newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany and Bosnia sign agreement on refugee return.
newsitem.headline: Germany and Bosnia sign agreement on refugee return.

text.p: Germany and Bosnia signed an agreement on Wednesday to repatriate more than 300,000 refugees from the conflict in former Yugoslavia and said they hoped many would start returning soon of their own free will.
But those who refuse will be sent back, starting with single adults and married couples without children, German Interior Minister Manfred Kanther said after signing the 13-page agreement.
"It has always been clear that when the war ended the refugees would have to go home and take part in the reconstruction of their country," he said in Bonn.
"We both agree that as many as possible as quickly as possible should go back voluntarily to their home," he added.

Bosnian Refugees and Displaced Persons Minister Nudzeim Recica, who signed the agreement for his government, told reporters the repatriation was of the "utmost importance" for the Bosnian government and Bosnian people.

"We have to start this process and we want our people back in Bosnia-Herzegovina," he said. "We need our people for reconstruction and for the reintegration of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state, as one state, as it was before (the war)."
Recica said both governments wanted as many refugees as possible to return voluntarily, but that other means would be found if they did not choose to go.
During the Balkan war, Germany welcomed more refugees than the rest of the European Union put together -- more than 400,000 from former Yugoslavia, 80 percent of them from Bosnia.

Germany's federal government and 16 states agreed earlier this year that refugees could be forced to go home from October 1 if they refused to go voluntarily. However so far, only a handful of men -- all convicted criminals -- have been sent home from the southern state of Bavaria.
The agreement makes refugee authorities in Bosnia responsible for receiving and caring for the refugees as well as resettling them around the country.
It also specifies that they will be sent back in phases.
Kanther said the first group of 70,000 to 90,000 will be back in Bosnia by June 30, 1997.
Some may be sent during the winter but the deadline allows the governments to wait until the weather warms up and still achieve this goal, a ministry official at the signing said.
Each state has its own policy on repatriating refugees, with Berlin and Bavaria taking the hardest line while some states have hesitated to crack down.
The majority of those who came to Germany are Moslems. Many of their homes are now situated in the Bosnian Serb Republic.

The Dayton peace agreement, which brought an end to the 43-month Bosnian war a year ago, promised the country's 2.5 million Moslem, Serb and Croat refugees and displaced persons a "phased and orderly" return to their homes.
As many as 250,000 may have gone back since, but few if any have crossed the boundary line Dayton drew between Moslem-Croat and Serb territory inside Bosnia.
NATO officers and U.N. officials agree the issue of returning Moslem refugees is so explosive it could undermine the entire Dayton peace process.

Recici said: "For us the return of refugees is the most important part of Dayton. The international community has to put pressure on those in Bosnia-Herzegovina who are not willing to accept the Dayton agreement and the right of people to return to their place of origin."
He said Western help with reconstruction should be withheld from those areas of Bosnia which refuse to comply with the Dayton accord.
